title: Taking Effective Notes
author: Jonathan Firth
summary: Jonathan Firth offers guidance on note-taking for new university students, framing it through memory and metacognition. Because working memory is limited, live note-taking forces multi-tasking, so teachers can help by leaving short gaps for students to review their notes. He says students often believe they should write lectures down verbatim, whereas the research favours capturing main ideas, which also encourages deep processing. Citing Kiewra and others, he argues that both taking notes and reviewing them help later performance, so students should be guided rather than told to just listen. For study outside class, re-reading, highlighting and time-consuming mind maps are weak strategies. He recommends quick tables, Venn diagrams or flow charts as a first step, followed by delayed retrieval practice to consolidate learning.
points: Working memory limits make live note-taking a multi-tasking problem, so short pauses for students to review notes during class are useful.
Students should aim to capture main ideas rather than verbatim wording, since identifying the gist is itself deep processing.
Taking notes and reviewing them each independently improve later assessment performance, and doing both is better still.
Re-reading, highlighting and mind-mapping give little return for the time invested compared with other strategies.
Organising notes into quick tables or diagrams helps understanding, but delayed active retrieval is what consolidates the learning.
quotes: Researchers tend to agree that it is preferable to aim for main ideas rather than the exact wording of lectures. In each short section of the lecture, students should try to capture the key thing that the speaker is trying to communicate.
The live nature of a class means that students are forced to multi-task; they have to think about, reorganise and jot down information on one idea while new information is still incoming.
Trying to make sense of new information and identify a main idea is also a form of deep processing, which can lead to better retention compared to a shallow strategy such as copying.
Each of these things (live note-taking & reviewing notes) independently benefits later assessment performance, and doing both is better still!
For this reason, it’s better to guide students on how to take notes rather than have them opt out entirely because they find it too difficult.
research evidence suggests that re-reading and highlighting a text are poor strategies, meaning that there is less to be gained for a given amount of time invested.

To resolve this, I’d still recommend that students organise new information e.g. into tables, Venn diagrams or flow charts, but that they aim for diagrams that are relatively quick to do, and see this as only the start of the process of learning the information – delayed active retrieval should be used to consolidate it.
